title: Kate Morgan Ghost Story at Hotel del Coronado, Explained
excerpt: She checked in under a fake name and never checked out. 134 years later, Hotel del Coronado still can't explain Kate Morgan.
content:
A woman calling herself Lottie A. Bernard checked into Hotel del Coronado on November 24, 1892, and five days later was found dead on an exterior staircase leading to the beach, a gunshot wound in her head. More than 130 years on, guests still request her old third-floor room hoping to feel whatever it is that lingers there.

The 24-year-old was actually named Kate Morgan, according to FOX 5 San Diego, which reports that hotel employees at the time said she appeared to be waiting for a man to join her. The San Diego County coroner ruled her death a self-inflicted wound, but the station notes some historians have disputed that finding ever since, and the exact circumstances of her death remain unclear. Before her identity was confirmed, local newspapers dubbed her the “Beautiful Stranger,” a nickname rooted in the fact that she had checked in under an alias and burned her personal letters in her room's fireplace before she died, according to Hotel del Coronado.

Morgan had checked in expecting company that apparently never arrived. Just before traveling to Coronado, the Iowa native had been working as a domestic servant for a wealthy Los Angeles family under yet another assumed name, Katie Logan, telling her employers she was taking a short leave to handle paperwork before she disappeared, per All That's Interesting.

A Suicide Ruling That Never Quite Stuck

The coroner's suicide finding has faced scrutiny for decades. San Francisco criminal defense attorney Alan M. May argued in his 1990 book, The Legend of Kate Morgan, that she was murdered, pointing out that the bullet recovered from her head did not match the caliber of the .44-caliber handgun she had purchased in San Diego, according to the Los Angeles Times. May reportedly spent years combing through medical and police records after staying at the hotel himself.

Identity questions have also lingered alongside the cause-of-death dispute. San Diego author John T. Cullen offered an alternate theory in his 2007 book, Dead Move, suggesting the woman who died was actually Elizabeth “Lizzie” Wyllie, entangled in a blackmail plot involving hotel co-owner John D. Spreckels, per the San Diego Public Library. Official records at the time identified the deceased as Morgan based on family contact and personal items, the library's account notes.

Morgan was buried in an unmarked grave at San Diego's Mount Hope Cemetery until 1989, when May purchased and dedicated a headstone that now sits in Division 5, Section 1 and draws visitors on local historic walking tours, according to Voice of San Diego.

Cold Spots, Flickering Lights and a Gift Shop That Won't Behave

Morgan originally checked into what was Room 302, later renumbered Room 3327 during the hotel's Victorian-era floor plan changes, and it remains the most requested guestroom among visitors hoping for a paranormal encounter, according to San Diego Magazine. FOX 5 San Diego reports that guests staying in Morgan's former room describe breezes that come from nowhere and a television that turns on and off by itself, while other visitors around the property report flickering lights, strange scents or sounds, and abrupt temperature changes.

The gift shop has its own reputation. FOX 5 San Diego reports that people believe the shop is haunted after watching items fly off the shelves and land upright and unbroken. Hauntings aren't confined to Morgan's old room, either: Room 3502 has drawn its own paranormal investigations, tied to a rumor that a hotel housemaid vanished the day after Morgan's funeral in December 1892, the Los Angeles Times reports, with parapsychologists testing magnetic fields and temperature drops in both rooms.

The hotel has leaned into the legend rather than shy away from it. Its Heritage Department published an official 2006 history book, Beautiful Stranger: The Ghost of Kate Morgan and the Hotel del Coronado, by historian Christine Donovan, documenting more than a century of reported sightings by guests and employees, according to Hotel del Coronado.

Ghost Tours Return for Halloween Season

Hotel del Coronado is running its Haunted Happenings tour again this Halloween season, a one-hour walk to places Kate Morgan once walked that includes stops tied to reported ghostly encounters around the property, per FOX 5 San Diego. On October 17, the resort will host An Evening With the Spirits, an event covering Morgan's story alongside séances, table rappings and Ouija boards, with access to her actual former guestroom. The hotel is also holding pumpkin carving events with carving and decorating supplies provided, bookable online, during the same season.

The activities arrive at a hotel that looks noticeably different from the one Morgan checked into, at least on the surface. Owner Blackstone Real Estate completed a $550 million multi-year restoration in June 2025 that revived the original 1888 Victorian front porch, lobby, stained-glass windows and central courtyard, according to Hilton, whose Curio Collection operates the resort. The resort's 138-year history also feeds into its holiday programming.

The Victorian beachfront resort, which opened in 1888 and was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1977, draws about a million visitors a year and has hosted celebrities, royalty and U.S. presidents, according to FOX 5 San Diego. It also served as a filming location for exterior scenes in the 1959 comedy Some Like It Hot, hosting Marilyn Monroe, Jack Lemmon and Tony Curtis during production, per a Medium account of the property's history. More than a century after Kate Morgan's death, the questions surrounding it remain as unresolved as ever.
